summary: The developer machine has the core tools and DocumentDB-specific MCP server and skills needed to build the FastAPI + LangChain sample against the provided cluster. Most cold answers were either outdated or confused with Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or Amazon DocumentDB; authoritative Microsoft docs (and the installed documentdb-* skills) clarify the correct resource types, CLI groups, connection-string shapes, capacity model, vector index syntax, built-in full-text and hybrid search, change-stream availability, and the open-source DocumentDB engine. The build can start, but the agent will need to pick concrete defaults for embedding/model choices, ensure vector-index dimensions match the chosen embedding model, and (optionally) add a missing accelerator (DocumentDB Agent Kit). A few local dev tools are not on PATH (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) — none block the sample, but adding mongosh would ease manual verification and some infra tooling would help if the repo wants to include IaC examples.
summary_points: Core build tools are present: python, pip (virtual env), node/npx, docker, az (signed in), the documentdb MCP server, and Microsoft Learn (learn) MCP server — so implementation and live verification against the provided cluster can start.

Many cold answers confused this managed vCore Mongo offering with Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU model) or other neighbours — the authoritative docs show the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster.

Vector search, hybrid search and full-text search are built into Azure DocumentDB (index kinds: vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann; search uses $search / cosmosSearch); the cold answer that recommended Azure Cognitive Search is incorrect.

Authentication for mongoClusters supports NativeAuth and Microsoft Entra ID (allowedModes), so token-based AAD flows are available for the cluster type — contrary to the cold answer saying AAD is not generally supported.

Missing accelerators: DocumentDB Agent Kit (would speed sample development). Missing but non-blocking CLI/tools: mongosh, bicep, terraform, azd, dotnet (add if you want local debugging or IaC generation).
Key builder decisions remain unanswered by the inventory/docs: which embedding model & dims to use and whether to implement async or sync pymongo client (affects code and index dims).

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Azure Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: The modern managed MongoDB-compatible cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2026-06-01 (deployment-language-arm-template)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and the older/common resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts used for Cosmos DB accounts; the model returned the older Cosmos account resource rather than the dedicated mongoClusters resource introduced for vCore clusters.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep or Terraform templates would deploy or target a Cosmos DB databaseAccount (RU model) instead of a dedicated mongoClusters vCore cluster; CLI commands, API properties, and billing model would be incorrect for the sample and could fail deployment or connect to the wrong resource.
improvements: Update quickstart and sample README wording to use the exact resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' when vCore clusters are intended (e.g., Quickstart and deployment docs).

Add a short deprecation note on the databaseAccounts pages or sample README where confusion arises: 'If you are creating a vCore Mongo cluster use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters instead of databaseAccounts.'

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: For Cosmos DB Mongo API: mongodb+srv:// or mongodb:// with host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and non-SRV port 10255; require ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters the connection strings are provided by the cluster (list-connection-strings) and commonly use mongodb+srv:// or mongodb:// forms but the hostnames look like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or related mongocluster suffix) and recommended options include tls=true (or tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256), retryWrites=false, and maxIdleTimeMS. The exact suffix and options are cluster-provided — use az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal to retrieve the canonical string. Do not assume the older .mongo.cosmos.azure.com/10255 shape used by Cosmos DB databaseAccounts.

grounding_links.title: Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (list connection strings) and connect docs
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Azure portal (cloud shell / mongosh examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts used hostnames like <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255; the newer managed mongoClusters use a different host naming pattern and connection-string options surfaced by az documentdb commands. The model conflated the two.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) is billed by Request Units (RU/s) and storage; not vCores.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB vCore-managed Mongo clusters capacity and billing are compute-tier (vCore-style) plus storage (example tiers: M30, M40 etc.). The RU model applies to Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (the RU-based Cosmos offering), not to the vCore DocumentDB clusters described by mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ComputeProperties.tier shows M30/M40)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared historical branding and the close relation to Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) caused the memory-based answer to give the RU-model billing mode (request units) rather than the current vCore / tier-based billing for mongoClusters.
confusions.build_risk: Selecting RU-based capacity or following RU-based provisioning guidance would produce templates and cost estimates that don't match the actual vCore billing and limits of mongoClusters; the sample might choose wrong tiers or miss limits for vector indexes.
improvements: Add a short section in the sample README: 'This sample targets a vCore DocumentDB cluster (Mxx tiers). Do not follow Cosmos RU-based provisioning examples.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary authentication is username/password via MongoDB SCRAM; Microsoft Entra ID token-based auth is not generally supported for MongoDB API data plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: mongoClusters support 'NativeAuth' (SCRAM) and 'MicrosoftEntraID' authentication modes (see AuthConfigProperties.allowedModes in the mongoClusters ARM docs). Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is supported for mongoClusters when the cluster's auth modes are configured to include MicrosoftEntraID (see the AuthConfig/allowedModes property in the mongoClusters docs).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (AuthConfigProperties.allowedModes includes MicrosoftEntraID and NativeAuth)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected older guidance for Cosmos DB or incomplete memory about AAD support; the mongoClusters resource explicitly documents allowed authentication modes including MicrosoftEntraID.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD isn't available they might implement only SCRAM credential flows, missing the recommended enterprise flow for Entra ID in some deployments, or they might incorrectly instruct users on how to create credentials.
improvements: Add a note in the security skill and the sample README showing how to configure allowedModes: ['NativeAuth','MicrosoftEntraID'] and link to the mongoClusters AuthConfig docs.
Provide a short code snippet in the driver skill demonstrating acquiring an AAD token and using it if MicrosoftEntraID is enabled.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Guessed 'knnVector' index and MongoDB-style knnVector options (indexType 'hnsw', 'ivf', 'diskann').
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes (kinds: vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann) and vector index creation uses the service-specific 'createIndexes' command with 'cosmosSearch' or 'cosmosSearchOptions' fields in the index definition (examples in the integrated vector store docs). The vector query operator is the $search stage with the cosmosSearch operator. The precise index kind strings and options are: 'vector-ivf', 'vector-hnsw', 'vector-diskann', with parameters like dimensions, similarity, numLists (IVF), m/efConstruction (HNSW), lBuild/lSearch/maxDegree (DiskANN).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector index kinds and examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model guessed MongoDB 7-style knnVector index syntax (knnVector) (common in MongoDB 7/Atlas) instead of the DocumentDB-specific 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' / 'vector-*' index kinds used in Azure DocumentDB. Shared terminology around HNSW/IVF/DiskANN caused the overlap.

improvements: Include a short example in vector-skill docs showing the exact createIndexes payload for IVF/HNSW/DiskANN and the $search aggregation stage using cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) to index Cosmos DB documents and perform full-text/hybrid searches.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect for Azure DocumentDB: full-text search is integrated into Azure DocumentDB (preview feature) via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25); hybrid BM25 + vector fusion is supported using server-side RRF or by combining $search pipelines with $unionWith and vector cosmosSearch. You do not need Azure Cognitive Search for integrated full-text or hybrid search with DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB users often pair Cosmos (SQL API) with Azure Cognitive Search for full-text needs historically; the cold answer reflected that older/other-product pattern rather than the integrated full-text and hybrid capabilities in DocumentDB.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB design patterns (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wired a separate Azure Cognitive Search index instead of using native createSearchIndexes and $search, they'd add unnecessary infrastructure and complexity and miss features that the integrated search provides (server-side RRF and tight hybrid queries).
improvements: Document the integrated full-text and hybrid search capability prominently on the quickstart and vector-search pages to reduce recommendations to use Azure Cognitive Search.
Add a sample that shows server-side RRF / $unionWith fusion as the preferred in-cluster hybrid example so builders use one cluster rather than two services.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports various server compatibility settings (3.2–7.0 historically) and not all MongoDB features are supported; check account serverVersion.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct in spirit: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (per compatibility docs). Most MongoDB operators (99.03%) are supported; some administrative commands and a very small set of aggregation stages/diagnostic/plan-cache commands are limited or unsupported — the official compatibility pages enumerate exact limitations.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: No full local emulator reliably supports the MongoDB API; run official MongoDB docker (port 27017) and test against the real Cosmos account for final verification.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is an open-source DocumentDB gateway/dev image and recommended local gateway usage: the DocumentDB gateway Docker image exposes the gateway on port 10260 for local dev (connection string mongodb://<user>:<password>@localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true). There are also Azure Local / Arc options and a Kubernetes operator for local evaluations. The Azure Cosmos DB emulator historically did not fully support MongoDB API; but the DocumentDB open-source gateway image is available for local testing.

confusions.build_risk: Builder who follows the cold answer may not provide the local gateway sample or .env.example for the DocumentDB gateway scenario; they might include only MongoDB-based local instructions leading to mismatch with cluster features (vector indexes) and TLS/cert handling.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Support for MongoDB change streams in Cosmos DB has been evolving; many versions did not support it. You must check account compatibility; there is no universal flag.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams ARE supported; Azure DocumentDB supports change streams and provides guidance on enabling the feature for multishard clusters (there is a 'Change streams' feature that can be enabled in the portal or via preview-feature flags). For migration and online scenarios, change streams are a supported mechanism and must be enabled/configured as required per cluster.

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Model.watch() uses change streams (docs show change-stream guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change-stream support varies by product and historically was not supported in some accounts; that uncertainty caused the cold answer to hedge. In contrast, DocumentDB explicitly documents change-stream usage and enabling steps.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable they may not implement the incremental summary-refresh path (relying only on batch rebuilds) and thereby miss a low-latency pattern supported by the service.
improvements: Add a short note in the documentdb-monitoring or migration skill about enabling change streams (portal/preview-feature flag) and include the example for Model.watch() and Azure Functions triggers.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB which was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: the historical Azure 'DocumentDB' (2014–2017) did become Azure Cosmos DB; however the modern 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' name replaced the earlier vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. The open-source DocumentDB project actually powers the modern Azure DocumentDB (it is related). Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is distinct from Cosmos DB (RU) and from Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (naming and relationship to Cosmos and OSS DocumentDB)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming facts)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple similarly named products and rebrands (original DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB; 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' -> 'Azure DocumentDB') and the open-source DocumentDB engine create overlapping names and historical ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: Documentation or README that uses inconsistent naming risks confusing users; builders might target the wrong API docs or CLI commands if they follow an older blog post or sample.
improvements: Standardize the naming in agent kit materials and the sample README to explicitly say: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) — resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; not Cosmos DB RU-based databaseAccounts.'
Add a short 'Terminology' section to the sample README that lists former names and where to look for the matching docs.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is the Azure Cosmos DB engine (not stock mongod). Most MongoDB drivers and apps work unchanged but expect some differences; test for unsupported commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB the engine is the open-source DocumentDB engine (built on PostgreSQL) that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. Applications can use standard MongoDB drivers unchanged for most operations, but there are documented differences and a small set of unsupported admin/diagnostic commands; builders should run the compatibility assessment and test their workload. The claim 'Cosmos DB engine' is misleading for modern DocumentDB which is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The long history of Microsoft product naming (earlier DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB) plus the presence of multiple managed Mongo offerings caused the cold answer to conflate engine names. The modern managed vCore product explicitly references the open-source DocumentDB engine.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos DB internal engine may lead builders to copy Cosmos-specific admin or connection patterns that don't apply to the DocumentDB engine; however, application-level MongoDB drivers and typical operations remain compatible.
improvements: Clarify in docs and agent skills that 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine' and provide a short compatibility checklist for common admin commands that differ.

confusions.question: What collections and indexes does the branch-performance sample need?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: transactions and branch_summaries; indexes on branch_id and transaction_time; vector index on summary_embedding using knnVector-like syntax (dimensions 1536, hnsw).
confusions.grounded_answer: The collection choices (transactions and branch_summaries) are appropriate; indexing guidance should be DocumentDB-specific: create single-field or compound indexes on branch_id and transaction_time via createIndexes, and if using vector embeddings on branch_summaries use DocumentDB vector index kinds (vector-hnsw / vector-diskann / vector-ivf) with the dimensions matching the chosen embedding model. Example vector-index creation uses the 'createIndexes' command and 'cosmosSearchOptions' with 'kind': 'vector-hnsw' (or 'vector-diskann'/'vector-ivf'), not 'knnVector'.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds and options)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed correct collection/index names with a MongoDB 7 knnVector syntax guess for vector index creation; DocumentDB uses 'vector-*' kinds with cosmosSearchOptions.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder creates the wrong index type or mismatched dimensions for embeddings the vector search will fail or behave incorrectly. The builder must choose an embedding model (dimensions) first and then create the matching vector index type and dimensions on the cluster.
improvements: Include a one-line recipe in the sample README: 'If you plan to enable LangChain embeddings, pick an embedding model (e.g., text-embedding-3-small => dims X) and create a vector index with kind vector-hnsw or vector-diskann and dimensions set appropriately.'

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline and $facet stages will compute volume, average ticket, and product mix per branch?
confusions.cold_answer: Provide an example $facet pipeline with grouping by branch_id and product sub-pipeline to compute product mix; store facet output per branch into branch_summaries.
confusions.grounded_answer: The proposed approach is sound: use an aggregation pipeline with $match (time window), $facet containing a byBranch pipeline (grouping with $sum, $avg) and a productMix pipeline (group by branch+product then regroup per branch) and project into a branch summary document. Store the results into branch_summaries with upsert/replace_one. This matches DocumentDB aggregation semantics and $facet usage.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & vector dimension

information_gaps.title: Driver style: async vs sync Python client
information_gaps.description: The prompt/skills do not mandate whether to use synchronous pymongo or async motor/AsyncIOMotorClient for FastAPI endpoints. The documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills give connection patterns but don't force a default. The builder must decide; I checked the driver skill docs, no explicit sample-level recommendation was found.

information_gaps.title: Recommended embedding & LLM provider env var names
information_gaps.description: No skill or doc prescribes exact environment variable names for embedding and chat model credentials (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY vs AZURE_OPENAI_KEY) or a default in .env.example. I searched the skills and Learn docs but found only guidance to store keys in env and not in files.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset size and idempotency
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks to seed sample data but not how large or whether the seed script must be idempotent. guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (ARM/Bicep/Terraform via AzAPI) for vCore-managed Mongo clusters and use az documentdb mongocluster ... CLI commands to inspect/create clusters; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb for vCore clusters.

Read the cluster-provided connection string at runtime from DOCUMENTDB_URI (as the sample prompt requires); do not hardcode host suffixes, ports (10255), or replicaSet values that apply to older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts — instead, call az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or use the portal to get the canonical string.
